Plain-English Summary of Section 7 — Indemnification and Limitation of Liability

Overall meaning: This section says when one side has to protect the other from outside legal claims, how that process works, and how much each side can be financially responsible for if something goes wrong.

Simple Summary

Both parties agree to protect the other if a third party makes certain kinds of legal claims. If one party breaks the agreement, acts with serious carelessness, acts intentionally wrong, or provides work that wrongly uses someone else’s intellectual property, that party must cover the other side’s related losses and legal costs.

There are limits to that protection. A party does not have to cover an intellectual property claim if the other side changed the deliverables, combined them with outside materials that caused the problem, or used them in a way the agreement did not allow.

If a claim happens, the protected party must notify the other side promptly, let that other side control the defense and settlement, and reasonably help with the case. But the defending party cannot settle in a way that admits fault for the protected party or forces the protected party to do something non-monetary unless the protected party agrees in writing.

The contract also limits liability. In most cases, neither side can recover indirect or hard-to-measure damages like lost profits, lost revenue, lost goodwill, or lost data. Also, except for certain serious categories, each party’s total financial liability is capped at the higher of:

  • the fees the customer paid or owed in the 12 months before the first event that caused liability, or
  • $100,000.

The liability cap and damage exclusions do not apply to certain important issues, including indemnification duties, confidentiality breaches, gross negligence, willful misconduct, and infringement of the other party’s intellectual property rights.

What This Means in Practical Terms

  • If one side causes a serious legal problem, that side generally pays for the fallout.
  • The protected side must hand over control of the legal defense, with some safeguards.
  • Big categories of knock-on damages are excluded in most disputes.
  • Most financial exposure is capped, but the cap does not protect a party from the most serious types of wrongdoing listed in the section.

Key Legal Terms in Plain Language

Indemnify: To pay the other side back, or protect them financially, for certain claims, losses, or damages.

Defend: To take responsibility for handling the legal defense of a claim, usually including hiring lawyers and managing the case.

Hold harmless: To shield the other side from having to bear the cost or legal burden of a covered claim.

Indemnifying Party: The party that must defend and pay when a covered claim falls within its responsibility.

Indemnified Parties: The people or entities being protected, including the other party and its officers, directors, employees, and agents.

Third-party claim: A claim brought by someone outside the contract, not by one of the two parties to the agreement.

Representation: A statement of fact one party says is true.

Warranty: A promise that certain facts, conditions, or performance standards are true or will be met.

Covenant: A promise in the contract that a party will do, or not do, something.

Gross negligence: More than ordinary carelessness; a very serious failure to use reasonable care.

Willful misconduct: Intentional wrongdoing, or acting with knowing disregard for the likely harm.

Deliverables: The work product, materials, software, documents, or other items one party provides under the agreement.

Infringe / misappropriate intellectual property: To improperly use, copy, or take someone else’s protected creations, such as copyrights, patents, trademarks, or trade secrets.

Scope expressly permitted under this Agreement: The specific ways the contract says the deliverables may be used. Using them outside those allowed ways can remove protection.

Promptly notify: Inform the other side without unreasonable delay.

Materially prejudiced: Meaningfully harmed in a practical way. Here, late notice only excuses the defending party if the delay actually hurt its ability to handle the claim.

Sole control of the defense and settlement: One party gets to manage the lawsuit and settlement discussions by itself, subject to the limits stated in the contract.

Non-monetary obligation: A requirement to do something other than pay money, such as admit fault, change business practices, or stop using something.

Indirect, incidental, consequential, special, punitive, or exemplary damages: Categories of damages that go beyond direct out-of-pocket harm, such as ripple-effect losses, penalties, or punishment-style awards.

Lost profits / lost revenue / loss of goodwill / loss of data: Financial or business harm from missed earnings, damaged reputation, or missing information.

Total cumulative liability: The maximum total amount one party can owe under the agreement for covered claims, added together.

Liability cap: The contractual maximum amount one party can be required to pay, except where the contract says the cap does not apply.
